blocks.prompt: The Bird That Has to Learn Its Song
blocks.text: A baby bird does not know its song. It has to learn it. First it listens. It sits in the nest and hears the grown up birds sing the same song again and again. The baby bird keeps that song in its head. Then it starts to practice. Its first tries sound wobbly and wrong, like a baby learning to talk. It practices for weeks. Little by little the song gets better. One day it sings the song right, and then it can sing it for the rest of its life.

blocks.prompt: The Song Nobody Is Born Knowing
blocks.text: A chicken hatches knowing how to cluck. A duck hatches knowing how to quack. But a songbird hatches knowing almost nothing about its song. It has to learn it, the way you learned to talk. Here is how it works. In its first weeks, a young sparrow listens to the adult birds around it and remembers their song. It does not sing yet. It just stores the sound. Later, when the bird finally opens its beak, what comes out is a mumbly mess. Scientists call this babbling, and it sounds a lot like a baby saying bababa. The bird keeps trying. It listens to itself, compares what it hears to the song stored in its memory, and fixes the parts that are wrong. This takes weeks of practice, sometimes thousands of tries. Then the song locks in. From that day on, the bird sings that song, and it stays the same for years. If a young songbird grows up alone and never hears an adult sing, it still sings. But the song comes out strange and broken, because nobody ever taught it.

blocks.prompt: Two Voices in One Throat
blocks.text: You make sound with your voice box, up in your throat, where two flaps of tissue vibrate as air rushes past. A bird does not sing with a voice box. Instead it has a syrinx, and the syrinx sits much deeper, right at the bottom of the windpipe, at the exact spot where the tube splits into two branches heading for the lungs. That location is the whole trick. Because the syrinx sits at a fork, it has two sides, and a songbird can control each side separately. A wood thrush can sing two different notes at the same time, then harmonize with itself. No human singer can do that. Some birds even use one side for the low notes and the other for the high ones, switching between them faster than you can hear. The syrinx is also remarkably efficient. A canary singing a long, fast trill takes tiny sips of air between syllables, dozens of times a second, so it never runs out of breath in the middle of a phrase. None of this comes free. A young songbird must still learn what to do with the instrument it was born with. It memorizes the songs of the adults around it, babbles for weeks, listens to its own mistakes, and slowly steers its two sided syrinx toward the remembered sound. A bird that is deafened before it finishes learning never gets there, because it cannot hear itself practice. So the next time you hear a bird outside the window, remember what you are listening to. That is an animal playing a two piece wind instrument buried in its chest, performing a song it had to learn by heart.

5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Vocal learning: hear it, store it, copy it
Only humans, birds, whales, bats, elephants and a few others do it
Subsong is a bird's version of babbling
Sensitive period: a window when the brain can absorb song
White crowned sparrows sing in local accents

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Learns a Language
blocks.text: Sound is easy to make. Almost any animal with lungs can force air past a flap of tissue and produce noise. Learning a sound is rare. Out of all the animals on Earth, only a handful can hear something, remember it, and then teach their own bodies to copy it. Humans can. Parrots, hummingbirds, and songbirds can. So can whales, dolphins, some bats, and elephants. That is nearly the entire club. Your dog cannot do it, and neither can a chimpanzee, which is an odd fact when you consider how closely related to us it is. A songbird learns like you did. In its first weeks it does almost nothing but listen, storing the songs of the adults nearby in memory. This window does not stay open forever. In many species there is a sensitive period, a stretch of early life when the brain is ready to absorb song, and a bird that hears nothing during that window will never sing normally afterward. Next comes the babbling. A young bird's first attempts are formless and rambling, and researchers call it subsong for a reason: it sounds startlingly like a human baby experimenting with bababa. Over the following weeks the bird practices, sometimes tens of thousands of times, listening to itself and nudging each attempt closer to the version stored in its head. Eventually the song crystallizes and stops changing. Because song is learned rather than inherited, it drifts, and it drifts by neighborhood. White crowned sparrows in one valley sing a noticeably different version from sparrows a few miles away. Birds in each area learn from the birds around them, small differences accumulate, and the result is a genuine local accent. Researchers can record a sparrow and often say where it grew up. There is a piece of this story that got told wrong for a long time. Biologists in Europe and North America mostly studied birds where the male sings and the female does not, and concluded that birdsong was essentially a male performance. Then researchers surveyed songbirds worldwide, including the tropics, where most species actually live. Female song turned out to be common, and the evidence suggests it was there from the beginning. The silent female was not the rule. She was a local exception that a few scientists mistook for the whole picture, because they were listening in the wrong place.

6.title: The Bird That Has to Learn Its Song
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Bird That Has to Learn Its Song

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Oscines: the true songbirds, roughly half of all bird species
The syrinx sits at the fork of the windpipe and has two sides
Stages: sensory, sensorimotor, crystallization
Zebra finches fix their song for life; canaries keep revising
Deafening after crystallization slowly wrecks the song
Female song is widespread and likely ancestral

blocks.prompt: The Song Is Not in the Egg
blocks.text: A chicken does not need lessons to cluck. A dove does not need lessons to coo. Those sounds arrive with the body, written into the animal in advance, and they come out correctly the first time whether or not the bird has ever heard another of its kind. A song sparrow is different. A song sparrow that never hears an adult sparrow will grow up and sing something, and that something will be wrong. The song is not in the egg. It has to be learned, and the learning looks remarkably like yours. Start with the instrument, because it is not the one you have. You speak with a larynx, a valve near the top of your throat. Birds have a larynx as well, but it is not what makes their song. They sing with a syrinx, which sits at the far bottom of the windpipe, exactly where the tube forks toward the two lungs. That fork is the point. A syrinx has two sides, and a songbird can drive each side independently, which means one animal can produce two unrelated notes at once and harmonize with itself. A canary running a rapid trill takes minibreaths between syllables, dozens per second, so the phrase never stops for air. The bird is not using a voice. It is playing a two piece wind instrument mounted inside its chest. The learning happens in stages, and the stages have names. First the sensory phase: a young bird listens to nearby adults and stores their song in memory, singing nothing itself. This window does not stay open, and a bird kept in silence through it is permanently marked. Then the sensorimotor phase, which opens with subsong, a rambling, formless babble that sounds uncannily like a human infant working through bababa. The bird then spends weeks converging on the memory, running tens of thousands of repetitions, listening to each attempt and correcting the gap between what it hears and what it stored. Finally the song crystallizes and stops moving. A zebra finch will sing essentially the same song for the rest of its life. A canary, an open ended learner, keeps revising and adds new material each year. The role of hearing is the part that shows the mechanism most clearly. A bird deafened before crystallization cannot converge, because it has no way to compare its output to its target, and its song stays a mess. More tellingly, a bird deafened after crystallization, one that already sings perfectly, slowly falls apart. The song degrades over months. It was never running on autopilot. The bird had been listening to itself the entire time. Because the song is transmitted by listening rather than by inheritance, it behaves like culture, and it does what culture does. It drifts locally. White crowned sparrows in one valley sing a version measurably different from birds a few miles off, since each generation learns from the neighbors it happens to have. These are dialects in the ordinary sense of the word, and a trained ear can often place a bird by its accent. One more thing, and it is a lesson about scientists rather than birds. For most of the last century the textbooks said that birdsong is a male display, sung to hold territory and attract females. That conclusion came from ornithologists working in Europe and North America, where the species around them mostly fit it. When researchers finally surveyed songbirds across the whole family, including the tropics, where the majority of species actually live, female song turned out to be widespread, and the evidence pointed to it being present in the common ancestor. The old rule was never a rule. It was a regional accent in the data, and the people writing it down had only ever listened in one valley.
